title: A first global standard on platform work
author: Editorial Desk
summary: The ILO opens negotiations on a convention for platform workers.
body:
In June 2025 the **113th session of the International Labour Conference** in Geneva held its first discussion on **decent work in the platform economy**. The aim is to negotiate a new international labour standard: a convention, which binds countries that ratify it, supplemented by a recommendation, which gives guidance. For the millions of people who earn a living by delivering food, driving cabs or doing tasks through an app, it is the first serious attempt to agree a global rulebook. This post explains why the step matters, what was decided, what remains disputed, and where India stands.

## Why this is a big step

Previous ILO standards were written for a world of factories, farms and offices, where the employer is a person or a company that can be identified, and where the place of work is a physical one. Digital labour platforms change that. Work is allotted by software, performance is rated by customers and algorithms, pay can change from one hour to the next, and the platform may be based in another country from the worker. The ILO has long had standards on freedom of association, forced labour, safety and discrimination, but none addresses the particular features of work through platforms. A standard would give governments, platforms and workers a common reference.

## What happened in June 2025

The Conference held its first standard-setting discussion on the subject, and a vote was taken on the form of the new instrument. According to a report by the international cooperative organisation CICOPA, delegates voted 1,480 to 1,064 in favour of drafting a legally binding Convention supported by a Recommendation, for possible adoption in 2026. The ILO itself reports that the Conference agreed that the outcome should be a Convention with a supporting Recommendation and set basic definitions and scope.

The negotiation did not finish its work. An employers' organisation report notes that after two weeks only about 15 per cent of the proposed text had been covered, and that a provisional agreement had been reached on several key elements, including definitions and the use of algorithms. CICOPA reports that many paragraphs of the draft Convention remain in brackets, which in ILO practice means that they are not agreed, and that they will be revisited in 2026. The ILO will prepare a consolidated report with updated legal texts as the basis for the second round.

The process runs over two sessions: a first discussion in 2025 to settle the form and main content, and a second in 2026 to finalise the text. A convention needs a two-thirds majority of votes cast for adoption.

## The questions under debate

The scope that has been proposed for the standard covers fundamental rights at work, fair pay and social protection, occupational safety and health, data protection and privacy, and access to dispute resolution. Within these headings, the main questions are:

- **Who is covered, and what is the employment status?** Should platform workers be treated as employees, as self-employed, or as a third category? Delegates also disagreed on how to define a digital platform and a platform worker. The planned approach is a principles-based convention that sets minimum standards, leaves room for national differences, and covers employees, the self-employed and contract-based service providers.
- **Algorithmic management.** Unions want workers to have a right to see how apps and algorithms decide their pay and hours and whether they can be removed from the platform.
- **Social protection and safety.** Who pays for insurance and pension, and who is responsible for accidents on the road?
- **Freedom of association and collective bargaining.** How can workers who are formally independent form unions and bargain with a platform?
- **Data protection.** Who owns the data that a worker generates, and how can it be used?

## The positions of the parties

The Employers' Group has said that the ILO should guide national laws and not legislate for them, and has expressed a preference for a principles-based approach that avoids excessive detail and can be adapted to national contexts. Employers have also warned that national and regional rules, and evolving court decisions, could make a new standard redundant or in conflict. The Workers' Group has said that it does not aim to oppose economic growth or innovation but wants decent working conditions extended to platform workers everywhere. Observers noted that the provisional language on definitions and algorithms tracks the European Union's Platform Work Directive, which suggests a growing convergence in how the issue is understood.

## India's position

The Government of India, employers' organisations and trade unions have all been consulted in the preparation. India has its own framework in the **Code on Social Security, 2020**, which defines gig workers, platform workers and aggregators and provides for schemes funded in part by aggregators' contributions. States such as Rajasthan and Karnataka have gone further with their own laws. This domestic experience is relevant, because a global standard must be one that countries with different systems can ratify.

BMS has urged that any global standard recognise the realities of developing countries, where platform work is a major source of employment and often an alternative to joblessness. The underlying point is that a standard has to work for countries where informality is widespread and platform jobs are for many young people an entry to income, while still giving the worker real rights.

## What it could mean for a worker

If a convention is adopted and India ratifies it, a delivery rider or a cab driver in an Indian city could expect, over time, some basic assurances. These might include the right to know how pay is calculated, a process to challenge a deactivation, safety and insurance cover, and a right to organise. None of this would happen automatically. Ratification would have to be followed by national law and enforcement, and in India the Code on Social Security and the State laws are the places where such rights would be written.

## What next

A second discussion at the 2026 Conference is expected to decide whether a convention is adopted. The ILO schedules the 114th session for 1 to 12 June 2026. Between the sessions, governments, employers and workers are expected to comment on the draft, and that is the time when unions in each country can give their views to the labour ministry. We will follow the outcome in this blog.
